# What Is Bytecode in Java?

## Objectives

After this lesson, you will be able to explain how bytecode differs from a `.class` file; describe how `javac` transforms source code into bytecode; recognize the basic structure of a class file; understand the operand stack, local variables, and JVM instruction groups; use `javap` to inspect bytecode; check the class-file version; and relate bytecode to class loading, verification, interpretation, and JIT compilation.

## 1. What is bytecode?

**Bytecode** is the intermediate instruction set generated by a compiler so that a runtime can execute it. In Java, bytecode is designed for the **Java Virtual Machine (JVM)**. The JVM reads bytecode, checks its validity, and executes it according to the JVM specification.

For example, the source code:

~~~java
int sum = 7 + 5;
~~~

can be compiled into a sequence of JVM instructions such as:

~~~text
bipush 7
iconst_5
iadd
istore_1
~~~

These instructions push two integers onto the operand stack, add them together, and store the result in a local variable. This is JVM bytecode, not direct CPU machine instructions.

### How does bytecode differ from machine code?

| Aspect | JVM bytecode | Native machine code |
|---|---|---|
| Execution target | Compatible JVM | Specific CPU/ISA such as x86-64 or AArch64 |
| Representation | JVM instruction set | Processor machine instructions |
| Architecture dependency | Not tied to a specific CPU | Dependent on CPU architecture |
| Verification | The JVM can verify structure and types | The CPU does not understand Java type rules |
| Execution | JVM interpreter and/or JIT compiler | Executed directly by the CPU |

Bytecode allows the same class file to run across different operating systems and architectures, provided there is a compatible JVM and the required dependencies. That does not mean every Java application automatically runs everywhere: class-file version, JDK APIs, native libraries, system permissions, and the deployment environment can still introduce differences.

### Bytecode is not Java source code

Bytecode has already been compiled from source. It does not preserve comments, whitespace, or original formatting. Some information such as local variable names and source line numbers can be stored in debug attributes, but this information may be stripped.

A class file can also be produced by another language on the JVM such as Kotlin or Scala. Therefore, a `.class` file is not necessarily generated from a `.java` file.

## 2. From source code to bytecode

Basic workflow:

~~~text
BytecodeDemo.java
       |
       | javac
       v
BytecodeDemo.class
       |
       | java / Java launcher
       v
JVM
       |
       +--> Load class
       +--> Link and verify
       +--> Initialize class
       +--> Execute bytecode
                 |
                 +--> Interpreter
                 +--> JIT compiler
                           |
                           v
                    Native machine code
~~~

**javac** reads source code, checks syntax and types, performs the required analysis steps, and generates class files. If there is a compilation error, the compiler does not produce a valid class file for the erroneous code.

**java** is the Java launcher. The launcher identifies the class/JAR/module/source file to run, sets up the environment, and starts the appropriate JVM. The JVM loads the class file, verifies, links, initializes, and executes the bytecode.

You should not assume that all bytecode is compiled entirely into native code as soon as the JVM starts. The JVM can interpret bytecode first, collect information about runtime behavior, and then JIT-compile methods or code paths that are hot enough into native code. The specific optimization strategy depends on the JVM and workload.

## 3. .class files vs. bytecode

These two concepts are related but not synonymous:

- **Class file (.class)** is the binary file format understood by the JVM.
- **Bytecode instructions** are the instructions stored inside a method's Code attribute in a class file.

A class file contains a great deal of metadata besides bytecode, for example:

- Class-file format version.
- Class name, superclass, and interfaces.
- Constant pool with constants and symbolic references.
- Field and method declarations.
- Access flags such as public, final, abstract, interface.
- Descriptors describing field types and method signatures.
- Attributes such as Code, Exceptions, SourceFile, Signature, annotations, StackMapTable, and debug information.

A single source file can produce multiple class files. For example, nested classes, anonymous classes, or certain compiler-generated constructs can produce files such as Outer.class and Outer$Inner.class. Conversely, a class file can also be generated by a compiler for another JVM language.

A JAR is a ZIP-based archive that can contain many class files, resources, and metadata. A JAR is not bytecode; it is a container holding class files along with other resources.

## 4. Basic structure of a class file

A class file has a binary structure defined in the JVM Specification. Its main fields can be outlined as follows:

~~~text
ClassFile {
    magic
    minor_version
    major_version
    constant_pool
    access_flags
    this_class
    super_class
    interfaces
    fields
    methods
    attributes
}
~~~

This is a conceptual outline, not Java source code.

### Magic number

The first four bytes of a valid class file are:

~~~text
CA FE BA BE
~~~

This is the magic number **0xCAFEBABE**, which identifies the class-file format. If a file is corrupted, downloaded incorrectly, or a non-class file is renamed to `.class`, the JVM can report a class format error.

### Class-file version

A class file contains `minor_version` and `major_version`. The major version indicates the generation of the class-file format produced by the compiler.

Common milestones:

| Java release | Class-file major version |
|---|---:|
| Java 8 | 52 |
| Java 11 | 55 |
| Java 17 | 61 |
| Java 21 | 65 |
| Java 25 | 69 |
| Java 26 | 70 |

For example, class-file major version 61 corresponds to Java 17. If a class file is compiled with Java 25 (major 69) but run on a JVM that only supports up to Java 21 (major 65), the JVM cannot load that class and may throw `UnsupportedClassVersionError`.

For class files that use preview features, the minor version can be 65535. These preview class files require a runtime of the matching release and the `--enable-preview` option; a preview class file from one release cannot be run as a preview class file on another release.

### Constant pool

The constant pool stores constants and symbolic references needed by the class file. Entries can describe:

- Class, interface, field, and method names.
- String literals and numeric constants.
- Field references, method references, and interface method references.
- Name-and-type descriptors.
- Method handles and method types.
- Dynamic or invokedynamic call-site metadata.
- Module and package metadata.

For example, a call to `System.out.println(...)` requires references to the `System.out` field and the `PrintStream.println` method. The class file stores those symbolic references in the constant pool; the JVM resolves them through linking when needed.

The constant pool is not just a list of literals. It is also the bridge between bytecode instructions and the names of the classes/members that those instructions need to access.

### Fields, methods, and attributes

The `fields` section describes the fields of the class: access flags, names, descriptors, and attributes. The `methods` section describes methods and constructors similarly.

For methods with an executable body, bytecode usually resides in the `Code` attribute. Abstract or native methods do not have a regular `Code` section because they do not have a Java bytecode body in the class file.

Attributes provide extended metadata. Some examples:

| Attribute | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Code | Bytecode, stack/local limits, exception table, and method attributes |
| LineNumberTable | Maps bytecode offsets to source line numbers |
| LocalVariableTable | Local variable names and types for debugging |
| StackMapTable | Verification type frames for bytecode verification |
| SourceFile | Associated source file name if recorded |
| Signature | Generic signature information |
| RuntimeVisibleAnnotations | Annotations retained so the runtime can read them |
| BootstrapMethods | Bootstrap method metadata for invokedynamic/dynamic constants |

Not every class file contains all attributes. Some attributes only appear when the compiler or tooling needs them.

## 5. The Code attribute and stack frames

A method's `Code` attribute contains key components:

- `max_stack`: maximum depth of the operand stack required by the method.
- `max_locals`: number of local variable slots required.
- `code`: sequence of bytecode instructions.
- `exception_table`: exception-handling information within the code region.
- Nested attributes such as `StackMapTable`, `LineNumberTable`, or `LocalVariableTable`.

When a method is invoked, the JVM creates a **frame** for that invocation. A frame has:

1. **Local variable array:** holds parameters and local variables.
2. **Operand stack:** where instructions pop operands and push results.
3. **Reference to the runtime constant pool:** supports symbolic resolution and operations on the class's constant pool.

Each method invocation has its own frame. When the method completes normally, the return value (if any) is passed back to the caller and the frame is discarded. When an exception is thrown, the JVM searches for a matching exception handler using the exception table and stack unwinding.

Local variables are accessed using instructions such as `iload`, `istore`, `aload`, and `astore`. The operand stack is used by instructions such as `iadd`, `imul`, `getfield`, `invokevirtual`, and `ireturn`.

This is a stack-based model: most JVM operations operate on the operand stack rather than specifying CPU registers directly as in native machine code.

## 6. Common groups of JVM bytecode instructions

The JVM has an instruction set defined in the JVM Specification. Instruction names typically reflect the data type or action.

### Loading and storing local variables

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| iload | Pushes an `int` local variable onto the operand stack |
| lload | Pushes a `long` local variable onto the operand stack |
| fload / dload | Loads a `float` / `double` |
| aload | Loads a reference |
| istore / astore | Pops a value from the stack and stores it into a local variable |

Example:

~~~text
iload_0
istore_1
~~~

Loads local variable slot 0 onto the stack, then stores that value into slot 1. Forms with `_0`, `_1`, `_2`, `_3` suffixes are shorthand instructions for common slots.

### Constants and arithmetic operations

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| iconst_0, iconst_1, ... | Pushes a commonly used small `int` constant onto the stack |
| bipush | Pushes a signed byte constant |
| sipush | Pushes a signed short constant |
| ldc | Loads a constant from the constant pool |
| iadd / isub / imul / idiv | Adds / subtracts / multiplies / divides `int` values |
| ladd / dadd | Adds `long` / `double` values |

Example:

~~~text
bipush 7
iconst_5
iadd
~~~

After these three instructions, the operand stack holds the `int` result 12.

### Control flow

- `ifeq`, `ifne`, `iflt`, `if_icmpge`: conditional branches.
- `goto`: unconditional jump.
- `tableswitch`, `lookupswitch`: implement `switch` branches.
- `ireturn`, `areturn`, `return`: exit the method and return the appropriate value.

Branches in bytecode use offsets to specify target positions. The compiler may translate an `if/else` or loop construct in source code into multiple instructions and branches.

### Field access and method invocation

| Instruction | General meaning |
|---|---|
| getstatic / putstatic | Read / write a static field |
| getfield / putfield | Read / write an instance field |
| invokestatic | Invoke a static method |
| invokevirtual | Invoke an instance method using virtual dispatch |
| invokespecial | Invoke a constructor, private method, or certain special calls |
| invokeinterface | Invoke a method via an interface |
| invokedynamic | Invoke via a call site linked by a bootstrap method |

### Object creation, type checks, and exceptions

- `new`: allocates an uninitialized object on the heap according to JVM rules.
- `dup`: duplicates the top value on the operand stack, commonly seen in object-creation sequences.
- `invokespecial <init>`: invokes the constructor to initialize the object.
- `checkcast`: checks and casts a reference; may throw `ClassCastException`.
- `instanceof`: checks whether an object is compatible with a type.
- `athrow`: throws an exception.

An expression like `new User("An")` in source code is typically compiled into a sequence of instructions containing `new`, `dup`, argument loading, and `invokespecial` to the constructor. There is no single bytecode instruction equivalent to this entire source expression.

## 7. Bytecode of a simple addition

Source code:

~~~java
public class BytecodeDemo {
    public static int add(int left, int right) {
        return left + right;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int result = add(7, 5);
        System.out.println("sum=" + result);
    }
}
~~~

The `add` method can be represented by the following core instructions:

~~~text
iload_0
iload_1
iadd
ireturn
~~~

Explanation:

1. `iload_0` pushes the `left` parameter onto the operand stack.
2. `iload_1` pushes the `right` parameter onto the operand stack.
3. `iadd` pops the two `int` values, adds them, and pushes the result onto the stack.
4. `ireturn` pops the resulting `int` and returns it to the caller.

For the `main` method, the compiler needs to load the two arguments `7` and `5`, call `add` using `invokestatic`, store the result, access `System.out`, construct the string, and call `println`. Details such as constant-pool indices, bytecode offsets, and string concatenation strategy can vary across compilers and JDK versions.

## 8. Creating and running a practical example

Create the file `BytecodeDemo.java`:

~~~java
public class BytecodeDemo {
    public static int add(int left, int right) {
        return left + right;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int result = add(7, 5);
        System.out.println("sum=" + result);
    }
}
~~~

Compile using JDK 17 or later while targeting Java 17 source/API and class-file version:

~~~bash
javac --release 17 -g BytecodeDemo.java
~~~

This command creates `BytecodeDemo.class` in the current directory. The `-g` option instructs the compiler to include debug information.

Run the program:

~~~bash
java BytecodeDemo
~~~

Exact output:

~~~text
sum=12
~~~

Use `javap` to inspect the bytecode:

~~~bash
javap -c -p -s BytecodeDemo
~~~

- `-c`: displays bytecode instructions.
- `-p`: shows private members as well.
- `-s`: displays internal type signatures/descriptors.

To view detailed structure:

~~~bash
javap -v BytecodeDemo
~~~

Verbose output includes the class-file version, constant pool, access flags, field/method descriptors, and attributes. The `major version: 61` line confirms the class file was generated for Java 17.

You can inspect the bytecode of a class inside a JAR by specifying the classpath:

~~~bash
javap -classpath app.jar -c -p com.example.Main
~~~

If `javap` reports that the class cannot be found, check the package name and classpath. `javap` is a disassembler for reading class files; it does not reconstruct the exact original Java source.

## 9. Reading method descriptors

In a class file, a descriptor describes the parameter types and return type of a field or method using JVM syntax.

Common symbols:

| Symbol | Type |
|---|---|
| Z | boolean |
| B | byte |
| C | char |
| S | short |
| I | int |
| J | long |
| F | float |
| D | double |
| V | void (return type only) |
| Ljava/lang/String; | java.lang.String |
| [I | int[] |
| [Ljava/lang/String; | String[] |

Example descriptors:

~~~text
(II)I
~~~

Means the method takes two `int` parameters and returns an `int`.

~~~text
([Ljava/lang/String;)V
~~~

Means the method takes one `String[]` parameter and returns `void`. This is the familiar descriptor of `main(String[] args)`.

Descriptors do not contain source parameter names like `left` or `right`. Parameter names can only appear in debug metadata if the compiler records them.

## 10. Bytecode verification

Before executing a class, the JVM checks whether the class file complies with the structural and type-safety constraints required by the JVM Specification.

The verifier checks many conditions, for example:

- The class-file structure and constant pool are valid.
- Bytecode instructions have valid opcodes and operands.
- The operand stack does not underflow or have an invalid type state.
- Local variables and the operand stack are used with compatible types.
- Control-flow branches and exception handlers have compatible stack states.
- Member accesses and invocations comply with the relevant access-checking rules.

`StackMapTable` can provide verification type frames at key control-flow points. The JVM uses these frames together with the bytecode to verify type and stack-state consistency. Class files generated by standard compilers typically include the metadata needed for this process.

Verification enables the JVM to reject malformed bytecode or safety-rule violations before executing the corresponding code. However, verification does not prove that an application's business logic is correct, does not prevent all logic bugs, does not guarantee the absence of `NullPointerException`, and does not replace security testing.

## 11. From bytecode to native code: interpreter and JIT

The JVM can execute bytecode in multiple ways:

### Interpreter

The interpreter reads bytecode instructions and performs the corresponding actions. This allows fast startup without compiling the entire application to native code up front.

### JIT compiler

The Just-In-Time compiler observes code as the program runs. Frequently executed methods or code paths can be compiled into native machine code to improve performance.

The HotSpot JVM has multiple compilation tiers and optimizations. The JIT can inline methods, eliminate certain checks when sufficient evidence exists, optimize loops, and leverage runtime profiling information. Optimizations depend on runtime profiles and can be deoptimized when assumptions no longer hold.

### Why should you not infer performance solely from bytecode?

Bytecode is only one part of the input to the JVM. Actual performance also depends on:

- JVM implementation and version.
- JIT compiler, tiered compilation, and profiling.
- Garbage collector and heap configuration.
- CPU, RAM, operating system, and container limits.
- Input data, concurrency, and workload.
- Libraries, I/O, network, and native code.

Two distributions can run the same class file with different performance characteristics. Even two JVM versions from the same vendor can optimize differently. Benchmark on realistic workloads instead of merely counting bytecode instructions.

## 12. Class-file version compatibility

A JVM only supports a specific range of class-file versions. When a class file is newer than the runtime, a common error is:

~~~text
java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError
~~~

For example: code compiled with JDK 25 produces major version 69, while the application runs on JDK 21 which only supports major versions up to 65.

### Using --release to choose the target

If you are using JDK 21 and want to produce class files compatible with Java 17:

~~~bash
javac --release 17 -d out src/BytecodeDemo.java
~~~

`--release 17` instructs the compiler to use the language rules, Java SE APIs, and class-file target of Java 17. It is safer than only setting `-source 17 -target 17`, because those two older options do not automatically restrict the platform APIs to the target release.

If the project uses Gradle or Maven, configure the Java toolchain and release target consistently in the build rather than relying only on whichever JDK happens to be in the terminal.

### Checking the class-file version

~~~bash
javap -verbose BytecodeDemo
~~~

Look for the `major version` line. Match that number against the version table above to determine the target release.

Preview class files require a matching runtime release and `--enable-preview`. A Java 25 preview class file is not a Java 26 preview class file.

## 13. Debug metadata and limitations of reverse-reading bytecode

The compiler can store metadata that helps debuggers and analysis tools map bytecode back to source:

- `SourceFile`: name of the source file.
- `LineNumberTable`: maps bytecode offsets to source line numbers.
- `LocalVariableTable`: name and descriptor of a local variable across a bytecode range.
- `LocalVariableTypeTable`: generic signature of a local variable if present.

Use `javac -g` to record full debug information. You can use `javac -g:none` to omit debug information.

When debug metadata is missing:

- Debuggers may not display local variable names.
- Stack traces still usually include the class, method, and line numbers if `LineNumberTable` is present; if not, the line number may appear as `Unknown Source`.
- `javap` still displays instructions, but it is harder to correlate them with source variable names.

Bytecode does not preserve comments, local variable names if not recorded, exact loop/conditional structures as written in source, or the original expression formatting. A decompiler can reconstruct approximate source code, but it cannot guarantee an exact reproduction of the original file.

## 14. Common misconceptions

### "Bytecode is machine code"

Incorrect. Bytecode is the JVM's instruction set. The JVM interpreter or JIT translates that behavior into platform-appropriate operations, which may include native machine code.

### "A .class file only contains bytecode"

Incorrect. A class file also contains the constant pool, class/member metadata, descriptors, access flags, attributes, and may contain bytecode inside each method's `Code` attribute.

### "Java runs everywhere because bytecode is platform-independent"

Platform independence only means the class file targets a compatible JVM. An application still needs the right Java APIs, dependencies, native libraries, system permissions, and configuration.

### "javap can recover the exact source code"

Incorrect. `javap` disassembles bytecode and displays metadata. It does not restore comments, formatting, or any variable names stripped by the compiler.

### "Bytecode verification guarantees a bug-free program"

Incorrect. Verification focuses on structural and type-safety validity of bytecode according to the JVM. Business-logic bugs, null data, race conditions, deadlocks, I/O errors, and many runtime issues can still occur.

## 15. Practical workflow for inspecting bytecode

1. Identify the source file or class file to inspect.
2. Compile with the appropriate JDK and target `--release`.
3. Use `javap -verbose` to inspect the class-file version and constant pool.
4. Use `javap -c -p` to inspect the instructions of each method.
5. Trace local variables and the operand stack to understand each operation.
6. Check descriptors to see parameter and return types.
7. Inspect `StackMapTable` and the exception table when investigating verification errors or control flow.
8. If the class is inside a JAR, specify the correct classpath and fully qualified class name.
9. Compare the runtime JDK against the class-file major version.
10. Use a profiler/JFR and benchmarks when analyzing performance; do not draw performance conclusions from disassembly alone.

## 16. Review checklist

- [ ] Distinguish bytecode from native machine code.
- [ ] Understand that `.class` is a binary container, while bytecode lives inside the `Code` attribute.
- [ ] Recognize the `CAFEBABE` magic number.
- [ ] Know class-file major versions and `UnsupportedClassVersionError`.
- [ ] Understand the constant pool, fields, methods, and attributes.
- [ ] Understand local variables, the operand stack, and frames.
- [ ] Recognize instruction groups such as load/store, arithmetic, branch, invoke, and return.
- [ ] Use `javap -c` to disassemble and `javap -v` to inspect metadata.
- [ ] Use `javac --release` to produce class files compatible with the target release.
- [ ] Distinguish bytecode verification from functional and security testing.
- [ ] Understand interpreter/JIT execution and avoid judging performance from bytecode alone.
- [ ] Know the limitations of debug metadata and decompilation.

## 17. Official references

- [Java Virtual Machine Specification, Java SE 26 — Chapter 4: The class File Format](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se26/html/jvms-4.html) — class-file structure, constant pool, Code attribute, verification, and attributes.
- [Java Virtual Machine Specification, Java SE 26 — Chapter 6: The Java Virtual Machine Instruction Set](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se26/html/jvms-6.html) — list of bytecode instructions and the semantics of each instruction.
- [javac — Java SE 26 Tool Specification](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/man/javac.html) — compiler options, `--release`, `-g`, and how class files are generated.
- [javap — Java SE 26 Tool Specification](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/man/javap.html) — how to disassemble and read class files.
- [Java Virtual Machine Specification, Java SE 26 — Chapter 5: Loading, Linking, and Initializing](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se26/html/jvms-5.html) — the lifecycle of class loading, linking, verification, and initialization.

Bytecode is the intermediate layer connecting Java source code to the JVM. Once you know how to read class-file structure, the operand stack, and instructions, you can understand what the compiler generated, diagnose class-file compatibility errors, and observe runtime details that source code does not show directly.
